name: Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
description: XSS flaws occur whenever an application takes user-supplied data and sends it to a web browser without first validating or encoding that content. XSS allows attackers to execute script in the victim's browser which can hijack user sessions, deface web sites, or redirect the user to malicious sites.
preventions: Encode all user-supplied output using the correct encoding for context.
Use a positive validation approach to accept known good input.
Implement Content Security Policy headers.

name: Injection Flaws
description: Injection flaws, particularly SQL injection, are common in web applications. Injection occurs when user-supplied data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The attacker's hostile data tricks the interpreter into executing unintended commands or changing data.
preventions: Use parameterized queries or stored procedures.
Validate all input against a strict allow-list.
Apply least privilege to database accounts.

name: Malicious File Execution
description: Code vulnerable to remote file inclusion (RFI) allows attackers to include hostile code and data, resulting in devastating attacks, such as total server compromise. Attacks can also target local files (LFI) and other URLs.
preventions: Use an indirect object reference map for file access.
Validate file types on upload; do not rely on user-supplied file names.
Ensure the web server cannot execute uploaded files.

name: Insecure Direct Object Reference
description: A direct object reference occurs when a developer exposes a reference to an internal implementation object, such as a file, directory, database record, or key, as a URL or form parameter. Attackers can manipulate those references to access other objects without authorization.
preventions: Replace direct references with indirect references per user or session.
Validate that the logged-in user is authorized for the requested resource.

name: Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
description: CSRF forces a logged-on victim's browser to send a pre-authenticated request to a vulnerable web application, which then forces the victim's browser to perform a hostile action to the benefit of the attacker. CSRF can be as powerful as the web application that it attacks.
preventions: Include an unpredictable token in every state-changing request.
Verify the Origin and Referer headers.
Use SameSite cookie attribute.

name: Information Leakage and Improper Error Handling
description: Applications can unintentionally leak information about their configuration, internal workings, or violate privacy through a variety of application problems. Attackers use this weakness to steal sensitive data, or conduct more serious attacks.
preventions: Use generic error messages for end users.
Log detailed errors only on the server side.
Remove debugging information from production systems.

name: Broken Authentication and Session Management
description: Account credentials and session tokens are often not properly protected. Attackers who can compromise passwords, keys, or authentication tokens can assume other users' identities and do anything they are authorized to do.
preventions: Use strong, server-generated session tokens.
Invalidate sessions on logout and expiration.
Enforce multi-factor authentication for sensitive operations.

name: Insecure Cryptographic Storage
description: Web applications rarely use cryptographic functions properly to protect data and credentials. Attackers use weakly protected data to conduct identity theft and other crimes, such as credit card fraud.
preventions: Use strong cryptographic algorithms (AES-256, SHA-256+).
Use proper key management practices.
Never implement your own cryptographic algorithms.

name: Insecure Communications
description: Applications frequently fail to encrypt network traffic when it is necessary to protect sensitive communications. Encryption should be used for all authenticated connections, especially internet-accessible web pages, but also back-end connections.
preventions: Use TLS for all connections that handle sensitive data.
Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.
Disable legacy protocols (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0).

name: Failure to Restrict URL Access
description: Frequently, an application only protects sensitive functionality by preventing the display of links or URLs to unauthorized users. Attackers can use this weakness to access and perform unauthorized operations by accessing those URLs directly.
preventions: Enforce authorization checks on every request.
Deny access by default.
Use role-based access control consistently throughout the application.
